title: Abstraction, abstract classes and interfaces
summary: Expose what an object does and hide how it does it. Abstract methods, abstract classes, Java interfaces (and default methods), how they differ, and how abstraction lets you swap implementations.
note:
1. Abstraction
   • Show **what** an object does, hide **how**
   • Callers depend on an interface, not on an implementation
2. Abstract method
   • `abstract void pay(int amt);` → no body in the declaring class
3. Abstract class
   • Declared `abstract`; has ≥ 0 abstract methods → **cannot be instantiated**
   • Can still have fields, constructors and implemented methods
   • A concrete subclass must override all inherited abstract methods, else it must be `abstract` too
4. Interface (Java keyword)
   • `interface` with abstract methods (implicitly `public abstract` pre-Java-8); since Java 8 also `default`/`static` methods; no instance state
   • A class can `implement` many interfaces (multiple inheritance of type)
5. Abstract class vs interface
   • Abstract class → shared base code/state for related classes (single inheritance)
   • Interface → a capability unrelated classes can share (many per class)
6. Abstraction vs encapsulation
   • Abstraction = hide complexity (design level) · Encapsulation = hide data (implementation level)
7. Why it matters
   • Swap implementations without touching callers (UPI ↔ card)
   • Basis of the Dependency Inversion principle (SOLID, LLD)
✎ In my words: ______________________________________________

recall.a: Exposing what an object does while hiding how it does it.

recall.q: What makes a class abstract in Java?
recall.a: The `abstract` keyword; it may have zero or more `abstract` methods and cannot be instantiated.

recall.q: Can an abstract class have a constructor and fields?
recall.a: Yes; its constructor runs when a subclass object is created.

An abstract class can hold state and shared code for related classes (extend one); interfaces declare a capability many classes implement (implement many) and, since Java 8, can carry default methods.
Abstraction hides complexity behind an interface (what callers see); encapsulation hides data behind methods (how the class protects state).

recall.q: What happens if a concrete subclass leaves an inherited abstract method unimplemented?
recall.a: It does not compile unless the subclass is itself declared `abstract`.

shot.title: Interface in action
shot.body:
```java
interface PaymentMethod {                     // interface
    boolean pay(long amount);                 // implicitly public abstract: what, not how
}
class Upi  implements PaymentMethod { public boolean pay(long a) { /* UPI */  return true; } }
class Card implements PaymentMethod { public boolean pay(long a) { /* card */ return true; } }

void checkout(PaymentMethod m, long total) { m.pay(total); }   // never changes
```
| | Abstract class | Interface |
|---|---|---|
| instance fields | yes | no (only constants) |
| implemented methods | yes | only `default`/`static` (Java 8+) |
| purpose | shared base for related classes | capability for unrelated classes |
| how many per class | extend one | implement many |

sections.title: What abstraction is
sections.body:
✍️ **Abstraction** means showing only the essential behaviour of something and hiding the details of how it works.
✍️ You drive a car through a steering wheel and pedals without knowing how fuel injection works; code calls `pay(amount)` without knowing whether it is UPI or a card.
✍️ In code, abstraction is achieved through **interfaces / abstract classes** (and also simply through well-designed methods and classes).

sections.title: Abstract methods and abstract classes
sections.body:
✍️ `abstract double area();` declares a method every concrete subclass must provide (no body here).
✍️ A class declared `abstract` **cannot be instantiated**: you cannot write `new Shape()`, but a variable of type `Shape` can reference a subclass object.
✍️ An abstract class can still have constructors, fields and normal implemented methods — it is a partial blueprint.
- Java methods are virtual by default, so an overriding method in a subclass is always dispatched dynamically; mark a method `final` to forbid overriding.
- Unlike C++, you do not (and cannot) declare a destructor; cleanup is the GC's job or `AutoCloseable`.

sections.title: Interfaces in Java
sections.body:
✍️ Java has the `interface` keyword. Before Java 8 an interface held only abstract methods (implicitly `public abstract`) and constants (`public static final`); since Java 8 it may also have `default` and `static` methods with bodies.
✍️ A class can `implement` several interfaces, gaining several capabilities (`class File implements Readable, Writable`), even though it may `extend` only one class — this is how Java does multiple inheritance of type without the diamond problem.
- An interface cannot hold instance state; that is the main thing that still separates it from an abstract class.

sections.title: Abstraction vs encapsulation
sections.body:
✍️ Abstraction answers **what** a caller can do (design level: the interface).
✍️ Encapsulation answers **how** an object protects its state (implementation level: private fields + methods).
✍️ They work together: an interface (abstraction) is implemented by classes that keep their state private (encapsulation).

sections.title: Why it matters (and the link to LLD)
sections.body:
✍️ Code that depends on an interface does not change when a new implementation is added — add `class Wallet implements PaymentMethod` and `checkout` stays the same.
✍️ This is the **Dependency Inversion** principle (the D in SOLID): depend on abstractions, not on concrete classes. It is the foundation of most LLD designs.
- It also makes testing easy: pass a fake implementation of the interface (or a mock).

sections.title: Interview questions
sections.body:
✍️ **Q: Can you create an object of an abstract class or interface?** No; but a reference of that type can point to a concrete subclass/implementor.
✍️ **Q: Can an abstract class have a constructor?** Yes, to initialise its own part of a subclass object.
✍️ **Q: When would you choose an abstract class over an interface?** When related classes share state or code; an interface when unrelated classes share only a capability, or when you need to implement several.
- **Q: Give a real example of abstraction.** A payment gateway, a logger with file/console back-ends, a database driver (JDBC).
